title: How can we be sure a five by seven grid cannot be tiled?
description: A grid of five rows and seven columns has thirty five squares, and every tile covers two. Any number of tiles covers an even number of squares, and thirty five is odd, so one reason settles every arrangement. Keeko's doubt, that a clever arrangement will fit, is struck.
teaching_notes: One idea: tiles always cover an even number of squares, so an odd count of squares can never be covered. Watch for students who keep trying arrangements instead of finding a reason.

source: Prove that a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.
video_script.why: The child sees that one counting reason shows no arrangement can work.
video_script.substitution: Each tile covers two squares, so n tiles cover two times n squares, always even.
video_script.anchor: A grid of unit squares with 5 rows and 7 columns, and a tile that covers 2 squares.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks a clever arrangement will fit if we keep trying. But there are far too many arrangements to try them all, so we need one reason that covers every arrangement.
video_script.payoff_line: No, the grid cannot be tiled, because thirty five is odd.

final_answer.value: Not possible: tiles always cover an even number of squares, and 35 is odd
final_answer.spoken: not possible, because tiles always cover an even number of squares, and thirty five is odd

hold_back: Not possible: tiles always cover an even number of squares, and 35 is odd
maths_rules: Each tile covers exactly 2 unit squares, with no overlap.
n tiles cover 2 × n squares, an even number, so any number of tiles covers an even number of squares.
35 is odd, so tiles cannot cover it exactly. There is no tiling of the 5 × 7 grid.
Slip: trying more and more arrangements can never prove that none works.
video_script.design: One grid and one tile. The squares are counted, then paired off with one left over. The slip is trying arrangement after arrangement.
